target_claim_or_section: §3 'lowest defensible capital for a self-sustaining business is about $4-5M' (ER-7 P50 $5.06M; P10 $4.03M)
challenge: The headline is the P10-P50 band of a route whose partner existence is unverified. P90 is $6.78M, the adverse case is a $11.4M floor that never turns positive, and the Monte Carlo does not price the chance that no partner exists. Rerunning Routes.fs to 180 months gives an ER-7 adverse deficit of $22.6M, still not cash-positive. An investor would read '$4-5M' as the raise size, but it is the optimistic half of a distribution that is itself conditional on a partner existing.
evidence: results.md §12: ER-7 P90 6.78M; adverse 11.43M not within 60. 15 §3 'Low confidence; channel partner unverified'. Rerun of Routes.fs logic at 180 months: ER-7 adverse capital $22.6M, never positive.
proposed_change: State capital as conditional: P(partner) x ER-7 + (1-P(partner)) x ER-4/pause. Quote P50-P90 ($5.1-6.8M) plus an explicit adverse figure. Replace 'about $4-5M' with 'about $5-7M if a partner signs; $6.5-14M+ direct'.

target_claim_or_section: §12 MC P10/P50/P90 capital percentiles for all routes
challenge: The percentiles mix full capital figures with draws truncated at 60 months: 12.7% of ER-7 draws, 18% of ER-4, 61% of ER-6 and 99.7% of ER-2 are 60-month deficits, not totals. A percentile over right-censored values is biased low, and the bias is largest in the upper tail (P90) that an investor uses to size reserves. For ER-2 the 'capital' P50 of $1.80M is just 60 months of burn.
evidence: Routes.fs simulate: Capital = -min(cumulative) over the horizon only; results.md §12 'Share never cash-positive' column. Rerun at 180 months: ER-1 base capital stays $2.0M but ER-2 base rises to $4.8M and keeps growing.
proposed_change: Either extend the horizon (e.g. 120-180 months) and report the share still negative, or report percentiles only over draws that reach cash-positive alongside P(never). Flag censored percentiles explicitly in 15 §2.

target_claim_or_section: §2 ER-2 (and ER-1/ER-3/ER-6 base) reported in the 'Capital' column
challenge: ER-2 is non-recurring. The model books a constant newCustomers x revenue each month: base 4/yr x $50k x 0.65 = $130k a year against $384k burn. It can never be cash-positive at any horizon, so its 'capital' of $1.87M is purely a function of the 60-month horizon. ER-1 base turns positive only in month 68 and repays in month 143; ER-6 base turns positive in month 73 and repays in month 152. The asterisk note ('a floor, not a total') is correct but understated: for ER-2 there is no total.
evidence: Routes.fs monthly(): non-recurring revenue = newCustomers*RevenuePerCustomer (no accumulation). Rerun with entry-routes.csv base values: ER-2 180-month deficit $4.8M, never positive; ER-1 positive month 68, payback month 143; ER-6 positive month 73, payback month 152.
proposed_change: Report ER-2 as 'never self-funding; annual net cost ~$0.25M' instead of a capital figure. For ER-1/ER-6, report the first positive month and the payback month beyond 60 months.

target_claim_or_section: §2 G2 'Licensed platform via channel' and ER-7 as the self-sustaining destination
challenge: This is not a venture-scale outcome even if everything works. ER-7 base reaches 11.25 customers x $300k = about $3.4M ARR at month 60. Cumulative cash at month 60 is still -$4.1M, and cumulative payback comes in month 89. ER-4 direct pays back in month 99. With no growth acceleration in the model, the business looks like a small lifestyle or PE-style software company, so a seed or Series A investor has no path to the 10x+ outcome their model requires.
evidence: results.md §12 ER-7 base: customers at 60 = 11.25, cumulative -4.12M; ER-4 base cumulative -5.82M. Rerun: ER-7 base payback month 89, ER-4 month 99; ER-7 base ARR month 180 ~$12.4M.
proposed_change: Add an explicit 'outcome scale' section: ARR at years 5/7/10, payback month, and the implied exit value at sector multiples. State plainly whether the plan is fundable by venture equity or should seek strategic, grant or founder funding.

target_claim_or_section: §4 revenue potential: '10k-account sponsor worth $0.8-1.5M a year'; ER-7 basis '3-10k-account sponsors' at $300k each
challenge: $300k net to vendor at $81 x 0.7 implies about 5.3k accounts per customer, so ER-7 base needs about 60k licensed accounts from 11 sponsors by month 60 (about 41 by month 180). Sponsors with 3-10k accounts sit mostly in SEG-001 (82 national sponsors), which the package itself calls least mobile (1 of 26 left). Community foundations have a median of 46 DAFs, and bank programmes are small and distributor-held. The industry has about 1.78M accounts in total (2023), most held by in-house commercial sponsors that will never license. The serviceable pool of 3-10k-account licensees is probably a few dozen, so the model assumes a large share capture.
evidence: 12 §1 SEG-001/SEG-002 counts; entry-routes.csv ER-7 basis; NPT charitable-giving statistics: 1,782,281 DAF accounts in 2023 (nptrust.org). Routes.fs: customers accumulate linearly with no population cap.
proposed_change: Build a bottom-up serviceable account count (non-captive sponsors by account band) and cap customers in Routes.fs at a plausible share. Report licensing TAM in $/year (accounts x $57 net) rather than sponsor-asset dollars.

target_claim_or_section: §1 break-even base '$250k balance'; §5 'numbers fail below about $150k average balance'
challenge: The base case uses a $250k average balance, but industry-wide assets over accounts (~$251.5bn / 1.78M, 2023) give about $141k. That is below the package's own failure threshold of ~$150k. Mid-size sponsors may differ, but no evidence is cited that the target segment averages $250k, and the administration fallback (G3, ER-5) depends on it.
evidence: 15 §5; NPT 2023 statistics: 1,782,281 accounts and ~$251.5bn assets (nptrust.org charitable-giving statistics).
proposed_change: Rebase break-even on segment-specific Schedule D averages, and show the $141k industry average case alongside the $250k case.

target_claim_or_section: SEG-013 'Acquirer, not licensee' vs 16 §2 G2 / ER-7 channel-partner licensing
challenge: The package's own evidence undercuts the channel route. Administrators acquire rather than license (SEG-013). The only distributor precedent (SEI) already chose TIFIN. Purchase controllers are paid to stay (CLM-017). Product advantages are not observed purchase triggers (CLM-016). A partner that owns the customer relationship, support and pricing takes 30% plus all switching power. It can re-platform, build or acquire once the vendor is proven, so the vendor bears the R&D risk while the partner captures most of the value. The 30% share and $40k CAC have no source beyond an earlier repository's assumption (trackF-notes: CAC UNKNOWN).
evidence: 12 §1 SEG-013 and SEG-003 notes; 16 §1 CLM-016/017; data/evidence/trackF-notes.md 'No published CAC... UNKNOWN... assumes about 30%'; entry-routes.csv ER-7 cac 40000.
proposed_change: Model partner economics from the partner's side (what it earns vs build/acquire). Add a scenario with a 40-50% channel share, a minimum-commitment clause and partner churn. Treat 'partner acquires us' as the likely outcome and value it.

target_claim_or_section: §2 staged G0-G1-G2 cumulative capital ('~$5M P50 (ER-7)' at G2)
challenge: The staged totals are not additive in the model. ER-7 is simulated standalone from month 0, with its own $1.6M build and 15 months to revenue. In the staged plan, ER-7 starts after G0-G1 (about 12 months and $0.7-1.2M already spent), while ER-6 services never turn positive within 60 months (base) and keep burning unless shut down. The true staged cumulative is about $5.7-6.5M+ and comes 12 months later, unless the wedge build is credited against ER-7's build, which is not shown either way. So the staged strategy also delays the partner signal that decides whether the company is fundable.
evidence: 16 §2 table capital column; 15 §3 G1 $0.7-1.2M; entry-routes.csv ER-6 and ER-7 rows modelled independently; results.md §12 ER-6 base never cash-positive.
proposed_change: Model the staged path as one cash flow (ER-6 months 0-12, then ER-7 with explicit build reuse and ER-6 wind-down or continuation) and report its single capital figure and timeline.

target_claim_or_section: G1 exit '≥2 paying customers' and the evidence-first wedge as basis for the next round
challenge: G1 success means about $30-120k ARR from copyable services. Doc 13 rates the eligibility and charity data as parity, replicable in 6-12 months, with Candid as the paid incumbent, and HYP-013 expects incumbents to copy migration commitments. That traction is far below what a priced round needs to raise the ~$4-5M for G2, so the company would need to raise G2 capital on interviews and a term-sheet conversation. The staged plan risks running out of money between the evidence and the financing, rather than avoiding failure.
evidence: 22 §1 V-2/V-8 pass rules ($15-25k subscriptions); 16 §2 G1 exit criteria; 13 ADV-001 'Parity', ADV-013 'until copied'; entry-routes.csv ER-1/ER-2 revenue $15-100k.
proposed_change: Define G1 gates in investor terms (ARR, signed partner LOI with minimum volume, pipeline value). Size the first raise to reach G2 revenue rather than just G1 evidence, or state that G1 is grant- or founder-funded.

challenge: Exit paths are not discussed. The plausible acquirers are well capitalised: Ren (Bain/Valeas 2023; Great Hill growth investment, Oct 2025), TIFIN, Foundation Source (GTCR per deal databases) and Foundant. They can copy the wedges within 6-24 months (doc 13). Observed vendor-ownership events (Pinkaloo, iPhi, DonorFirst, Vennfi, Giving Place) are small tuck-ins, which suggests acqui-hire or tuck-in valuations, not venture returns. Selling the archive or migration adapters to Ren would also undercut the 'exit symmetry vs Ren' positioning.
evidence: Great Hill press release 2025-10-28 (businesswire.com/news/home/20251028702541/en); 07 'Vendor-ownership events' list; 13 replicability column; trackC-notes GTCR/Foundation Source.
proposed_change: Add an exit section: named acquirers, precedent deal sizes where public, which assets they would pay for (archive, adapters, customer contracts), and whether a tuck-in exit returns the capital at each route's raise size.

target_claim_or_section: §5 'Conditions under which the numbers fail' and 16 §6 'What would make this wrong'
challenge: Several investor-material risks are missing from the failure lists. (a) Team and key-person risk: no team, hiring plan or founder roles, and the $4.5M figure depends on below-market founder pay. (b) Echelon Foundry commercial licence terms for reused components are open (OQ-017 in doc 21) but absent from the capital and risk sections; IP ownership and assignability affect both fundability and exit. (c) Concentration: doc 12 §4 concedes any first customer is >25% of revenue for years, and ER-7 adds dependence on a single partner. (d) Liability and insurance cost for the 'eligibility evidence' that auditors rely on.
evidence: 21-evidence-gaps.md 'Echelon commercial licence terms (OQ-017)'; 15 §2 founder-led note; 12 §4; 13 §3 regulatory concentration (SOC 1 scope).
proposed_change: Add a risk register covering team/key person, IP chain of title and Echelon licence terms (must be resolved before a priced round), customer and partner concentration with contractual mitigants, and E&O/media liability cost in burn.

challenge: The cash model has no churn, no price compression, flat burn regardless of customer count (support and implementation do not scale except via variable share), no implementation lag between signature and revenue, and linear acquisition with no population cap. Every one of these flatters the licensing routes. A 10% annual churn on ER-7 alone would push payback well beyond month 89.
evidence: Routes.fs monthly(): customers = CustomersPerYear/12 x active; Burn constant; no churn term.
proposed_change: Add churn, a burn step per N customers, implementation lag and a population cap, then rerun §12 and the Monte Carlo.
